To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the bias humidity test 85/85 is not a real world application condition for thin film resistive components.
the bias voltage and humidity influence the drift rate in the same way.
the drifts of resistive thin films in a biased environment depend on the applied voltage and the temperature and humidity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new model for the prognosis of drift phenomena of thin film resistive systems under all environmental conditions and load.
the following questions: (1) How does the drift of thin film resistive layers depend on the bias conditions, i.e., temperature, relative humidity, and applied voltage?
the following questions: (1) Can the drift behavior of thin film resistive layers be described by an Arrhenius-type model?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the biased humidity test is a useful and meaningful test, which is not only a test for the reliability of thin film resistive systems, but is a test for their long-term stability as well.
the 85/ 85 test, which is a part of the qualification procedure of thin film resistive layers, can be a good basis for the prognosis of the time dependence of drifts in the field of use.
the bias humidity test is an important part of the thin film resistors’ stability test.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have been able to show that the 85/850 test is not a worst case for thin film resistor stability in the long term and that the time-dependent stability of thin film resistive layers is not linear in the temperature–humidity–voltage–time space.
the 85/850 h biased test is an appropriate screening test for thin film resistive components and that the 85 °C and 85% RH conditions are the most severe ones for drift.
we are able to give an answer to the question of how long the resistive layer of a resistor will keep its specified resistance value, even under the most severe conditions of use.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the bias humidity test 85/85 is not suitable for predicting drift behavior of thin film resistive layers in the long term.
it is possible to use Arrhenius-like models to predict the drift of thin film resistive elements under biased humidity test conditions.
it is possible to predict the drift of thin film resistive layers under any environmental condition and any load.
